children: By Laura Kreutzer

Welcome back! I hope everyone in the U.S. was able to enjoy a nice Labor Day weekend. This morning's newsletter kicks off with a story from our own Chris Cumming who examines the latest proposal from the Securities and Exchange Commission that would allow private-equity managers more leeway in their political campaign contributions, although not everyone thinks the proposal is a good one.

Meanwhile, our Journal colleagues Gina Heeb and Ben Glickman report that EverBank Financial has agreed to a reverse merger, laying a path for the bank's private-equity owners to eventually exit. Finally, the Journal's Kate Clark looks at the venture industry's newfound love of startups built around human experiences that cannot be easily displaced by artificial intelligence.
Read on for more on these stories and many others...
Today's Top Stories

The Securities and Exchange Commission is planning a change that would let private-equity managers spend more on political races, particularly at the state and local levels, Chris Cumming reports for Pro. The agency on Thursday proposed eliminating its sixteen-year-old "pay to play" rule, which bars investment advisers from being paid to manage money for government clients after making contributions to them, saying it restricts lawful political speech. The SEC's change could have the biggest impact at the state and local levels, attorneys say.

Private-equity backed EverBank Financial has reached a deal to pursue a reverse merger with a smaller bank in the Pacific Northwest, WaFd in a deal that would create a regional bank with some $75 billion in assets, the Journal reports. EverBank's private-equity owners, which have included Stone Point Capital, Warburg Pincus, Reverence Capital Partners, Sixth Street and Bayview Asset Management, had been exploring either selling or taking EverBank public, the Journal previously reported.

Venture capital is usually associated with moonshot technology bets. Lately, though, some venture investors have found new, more analog pursuits: sports teams, iconic real estate and even children's toys, Kate Clark writes for the Journal. Investors are looking for opportunities insulated from the AI boom, including businesses built around human experiences that ChatGPT can't replace. Josh Kushner, founder of investment firm Thrive Capital, is among those who have recently acquired stakes in some of America's leading sports franchises, including the San Francisco Giants and a $12.5 billion deal that made the Los Angeles Lakers the most valuable sports team ever.
Big Number
The total value of global M&A during August, the highest level for that month in five years, according to London Stock Exchange Group data.
Deals

European buyout firm EQT AB has agreed to buy a majority stake in specialty reinsurance broker McGill and Partners for $2 billion, the Swedish investment group said Friday. As the Journal reports, Stockholm-listed EQT will buy the stake from New York-based Warburg Pincus. The transaction remains subject to approvals, EQT said, and is expected to close in the first half of 2027. Warburg initially backed London-based McGill when it was founded in 2019 as a cornerstone investor. The business now generates more than $250 million in revenue, Warburg said.

European buyout firm CVC Capital Partners has invested in Unitex Textile Services, an Elmsford, N.Y.-based company that offers textile management services, such as linen rental and laundry processing to hospitals, nursing homes and other healthcare facilities across the Northeastern U.S. The founding Potack family retains a significant investment in the business and continues to lead it. Amsterdam-listed CVC invested through its strategic opportunities strategy.

Australian retirement communities and holiday parks owner Ingenia Communities has rejected a takeover proposal from Warburg Pincus that values its equity at 1.94 billion Australian dollars, equivalent to $1.40 billion, Dow Jones Newswires' David Winning writes.

Los Angeles-based firm Ataline Capital Management has backed its fourth platform in the past 12 months with a growth investment in Risk & Regulatory Consulting, which offers actuarial, financial, information technology and compliance consulting services to U.S. insurance regulators.

Venture investor Andreessen Horowitz led a $300 million growth investment in artificial intelligence startup Gimlet Labs. Bloomberg News reports that the transaction valued the company at $3 billion. Other investors in the deal include Sapphire Ventures, Menlo Ventures and Tiger Global Management, among others.
One Equity Partners is investing in railcar and locomotive maintenance and repair services provider Metro East Industries. The Alorton, Ill.-based company works with railroads around the U.S.

Buyout firm KKR & Co. is backing Malaysian provider Avisena Healthcare with a minority growth investment. The fresh cash will support the company's plans to build new hospitals and add medical specialties.
Truelink Capital has completed its acquisition of JT Thorpe Group, which offers industrial maintenance and thermal management services for infrastructure and industrial end markets.

European software investor Copilot Capital has acquired a majority stake in Green Eagle Solutions, which provides programs used to automate renewable energy operations, according to an emailed news release. The Madrid company supports projects in 18 countries. London-based Copilot invested from its first fund. The firm typically backs companies with EUR5 million to EUR15 million, or $5.8 million to $17.4 million, in annual recurring revenue.
Add-On Deals
Exits

The alternatives arm of Goldman Sachs stands to make 16 times its original investment in EPC Power with the $4.4 billion sale of the company to publicly traded Flex, a person familiar with the deal told WSJ Pro's Isaac Taylor. Goldman and private-equity firm Cleanhill Partners initially acquired the provider of power conversion products and services for data centers and power grid applications back in 2022.

ClearSky-backed controls engineering company Utility Innovation Holdings has agreed to be acquired by strategic buyer Vertiv Holdings for as much as $2.6 billion in cash, including about $1.45 billion at closing and up to $1.15 billion in potential earnouts. Raleigh, N.C.-based Utility Innovation focuses on microgrid engineering and security for behind-the-meter data-center power sources. The upfront price represents about 13 times the company's projected 2027 adjusted pretax earnings. Growth investor ClearSky in West Palm Beach, Fla., has backed the business as a minority investor since 2021, the year the company was formed, according to the firm's website.
Funds

Multistage venture-capital firm HOF Capital Management has raised at least $708 million so far for HOF Capital Strategic Opportunities II, according to a regulatory filing. The amount raised puts the fund nearly half way to a $1.5 billion offering amount indicated in the filing.

True Ventures has raised at least $172 million so far for True Ventures IX, which is seeking $225 million, and at least $56 million for True Ventures Select V, which is seeking $100 million, according to two separate regulatory filings. True Ventures' ninth fund focuses on early-stage deals, while its Select strategy is earmarked for follow-on investments in the firm's most promising early-stage portfolio companies.
People

A trio of nerdy Frenchmen came to New York to build a sassy chatbot for teens. A decade later, their startup has grown into an artificial-intelligence platform that is a pillar of the tech ecosystem, and a linchpin in the strategy of the world's most valuable company, the Journal reports. Nvidia agreed on Thursday to buy their AI company, called Hugging Face, for roughly $13 billion, doubling down on the chipmaker's effort to challenge the dominance of proprietary AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic. But when Clément Delangue and Julien Chaumond first arrived at the Manhattan offices of venture capital fund Betaworks for its "BotCamp" startup program in the sweltering summer of 2016, their goal was more modest.
Industry News

The Justice Department's antitrust division was instructed earlier this week to pause all work with the Canadian government, according to emails reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, the latest development in the escalating trade dispute between the two countries. In a Wednesday email with the subject line "Pause on Canada," Lynda Marshall, the chief of the antitrust division's international section, ordered officials to stop all cooperation on cases and engagement on policy issues with Canadian authorities. She provided no reason for the directive, but said she would "circle back if the guidance changes."
